HighLikelyImproper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') in app/db.py:set_receipt_templateCWE-94db.py
Description

set_receipt_template() stores the caller-provided template string into restaurants.receipt_template at app/db.py:74-75. The scanner flagged this because the stored value is described elsewhere in the project metadata as later being passed to Flask/Jinja render_template_string, which would treat the stored text as executable template syntax rather than inert content. This becomes a security issue if an authenticated merchant can submit arbitrary template text through the receipts editor and the application later renders that stored value in a normal Jinja context.

Fileapp/db.py
Line74
Impact (if exploitable)

If the stored value is later rendered as Jinja, a merchant-supplied template can execute template expressions in the server-side rendering context. The provided metadata states that order and restaurant objects are in scope during rendering, so the effect could include unintended access to server-side template context data and template-driven actions reachable from that environment. This is similar in pattern to prior Jinja-related issues such as CVE-2016-10745 in that attacker-controlled template text reaches a Jinja execution surface, although the supplied evidence does not show the specific sandbox-escape mechanism from that CVE.

Security impact
SeverityHigh

Likely exploitable with substantial impact to system confidentiality or integrity.

Weakness IDCWE-94View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Models voting true positive: 1
  • Models voting false positive: 0
  • The provided review transcript contains a single model assessment, so there was no multi-model disagreement to compare.
  • The true-positive argument was that raw request.form["template"] is stored without restriction and later rendered through render_template_string, creating a stored SSTI path.
  • The noted counterpoint was that receipt-template customization may be an intentional feature, and this function itself performs persistence rather than execution.
  • No unresolved technical disagreement was recorded beyond that design-intent caveat.

CVSS v3.1 base score 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, confidence: medium) — AV:N (app/routes/receipts.py:32-47 lets an authenticated merchant submit template text over HTTP, stores it via db.set_receipt_template, and then renders that attacker-controlled template server-side); AC:L (the template is accepted verbatim from request.form and rendered with render_template_string without validation or a special prerequisite); PR:L (the reachable entry point is /receipts under @login_required, so a merchant session is required first); UI:N (the attacker can submit the template and trigger rendering directly); S:U (the execution occurs in the application’s Flask/Jinja context rather than crossing into a different security authority); C:H (server-side execution of attacker-controlled template/code in that context can expose application data available to the app); I:H (the evidence shows attacker-controlled template/code execution via render_template_string, which is unauthorized execution in the app context); A:H (the same server-side execution capability can directly disrupt processing within that application authority).

Description

detail() loads a per-restaurant receipt template from db.get_receipt_template(user["restaurant_id"]) at line 36 and renders it with Flask's render_template_string() at line 43. The finding is based on the template text being merchant-controlled according to the provided trace, which states request.form["template"] is stored verbatim for that restaurant and later executed with order, restaurant, and total in scope. MediumLikelyMissing Authentication for Critical Function in app/auth.py:login_requiredCWE-306auth.py
Description

login_required in app/auth.py treats a request as authenticated when current_user() resolves a database row from session["user_id"]. The scanner flagged line 40 because this route guard relies on Flask session integrity, while the finding context states the application can fall back to a literal SECRET_KEY ("portal-dev-key"), making a forged signed session cookie a prerequisite for bypass. If deployment overrides that fallback with a strong secret, this decorator behaves as a normal session-based authentication check.

Fileapp/auth.py
Line40
Impact (if exploitable)

If the fallback secret is in use, an unauthenticated remote client could forge a session cookie that causes login_required to treat the request as logged in. The resulting impact depends on the wrapped route: it may expose merchant-only pages or permit actions available to the chosen account, subject to any additional object-level or role checks in those routes.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-306View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • True positive votes: 1
  • False positive votes: 0
  • Review limitation: the debate transcript shows a single-model review, so there was no multi-model disagreement to compare.

Arguments recorded for the finding

  • current_user() reads session["user_id"] at app/auth.py:32 and loads a user row at line 33.
  • login_required at line 40 only checks whether that lookup returns a user object.
  • The finding context states Config.SECRET_KEY can fall back to the known literal "portal-dev-key", and create_app loads that configuration, so Flask’s client-signed session cookie can be forged under that configuration.
  • Under those conditions, protected routes using this decorator can be reached without completing the login flow.

Arguments recorded against or limiting the finding

  • The decorator itself is a standard session check and does not introduce the predictable secret.
  • If deployment sets a strong MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET, the reported bypass condition does not apply.
  • The scenario also depends on Flask using its default signed-cookie session mechanism and on the attacker choosing a valid user_id.

Unresolved disagreements

  • No direct disagreement was recorded; the main limitation discussed was that exploitability depends on deployment configuration outside this function.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:N (the attacker sends a forged Flask session cookie to HTTP endpoints protected by @login_required); AC:L (when the app uses the fallback "portal-dev-key", minting a cookie with a chosen session['user_id'] requires no external condition beyond that vulnerable configuration); PR:N (the decorator accepts the forged session without any prior authenticated privileges); UI:N (no victim interaction is needed); S:U (auth.py and the protected merchant routes are within the same application and database authority); C:L (bypassing the decorator makes merchant-session routes that expose tenant menu, order, and receipt data reachable as the chosen user); I:L (the same bypass reaches protected editing/status-update routes that rely on this decorator as the gate for tenant changes); A:N (the evidence shows unauthorized access, not a direct service outage, from the decorator bypass itself).

Data flow

session.get("user_id") -> db.get_user -> current_user

  • [ENTRY] session.get("user_id") app/auth.py:32 current_user pulls user_id from the Flask session, which is attacker-controlled if the deployment keeps the documented default signing secret.
  • [FLOW] db.get_user app/auth.py:33 The session-derived user_id is passed to the database lookup, and any matching row becomes g.user without additional authentication checks here.
  • [FLAG] current_user app/auth.py:40 login_required uses the resolved g.user value as the route-level authentication decision.
Prerequisites
  • Deployment conditions
    • The application must run with the documented default SECRET_KEY fallback ("portal-dev-key") or another predictable signing key.
    • Flask session cookies must remain client-side signed tokens.
    • The attacker must be able to mint a valid session containing a chosen user_id, and that id must map to an existing user row.
  • Code inclusion
    • This is core application code in app/auth.py, not an optional or loadable extension.
  • Trust boundary
    • The relevant boundary is between public HTTP clients and authenticated merchant session routes.
    • The decorator is intended to enforce that boundary for wrapped views, but its decision is based entirely on session-backed identity.
  • Project context

  • Related CVE note
    • The listed CVE-2021-23336 concerns URL query parsing ambiguities in urllib.parse; it is not a close variant of this session-authentication finding.
Description

Treat this decorator as dependent on a trusted session layer. The concrete mitigation is in configuration rather than in login_required itself: remove the literal SECRET_KEY fallback, require a deployment-unique secret at startup, and invalidate or rotate existing sessions when changing the key. If that configuration guarantee is not present, routes relying only on this decorator inherit the weakened authentication boundary.

MediumLikelyUse of Hard-coded Credentials in app/auth.py:login_userCWE-798auth.py
Description

login_user() writes user["id"] and user["restaurant_id"] into Flask's default cookie-backed session at app/auth.py:22-23. The finding was flagged because repository context indicates the app can fall back to a known Flask secret ("portal-dev-key") when MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET is unset, which would allow a client to forge the signed session data that current_user() later trusts. This becomes a security issue if that fallback secret is present in a deployed environment and an attacker can supply or derive valid session fields such as user_id.

Fileapp/auth.py
Line22
Impact (if exploitable)

A client that can sign its own Flask session cookie could set user_id and restaurant_id values that current_user() and login_required() treat as authenticated session state. That could permit access to merchant routes and actions under another account, subject to the existence or guessability of valid identifiers.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-798View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Review outcome in the provided transcript: 1 model marked true positive, 0 marked false positive.
  • Main argument for the finding: the code stores authentication state in a Flask client-signed session, and repository context says the signing key has a deployment-known fallback; with that condition, a forged session can impersonate a user.
  • Main counterpoint raised in the transcript: deployments can override MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET, and the fallback literal is in config.py, not in login_user() itself.
  • Unresolved point: exploitability depends on runtime configuration and whether the fallback secret is actually used.
  • Limitation: the debate record shown here is a single-model review rather than a multi-model split discussion.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:N (the trigger is a forged Flask session cookie sent over the app's HTTP routes, and current_user later trusts session['user_id'] from that cookie); AC:L (once the fallback secret is in use, exploitation is just signing a cookie with chosen user_id/restaurant_id, with no race or target-specific condition shown); PR:N (the shared boundary says public HTTP routes are reachable without prior authentication, and the finding's trigger is an attacker-crafted cookie); UI:N (no separate victim action is needed because the attacker submits the forged cookie directly); S:U (the forged session is consumed by the same Flask application and authority that stores and trusts the session state); C:L (accepting forged auth-bearing session state directly grants unauthorized access to authenticated merchant data exposed behind the session-backed routes); I:L (the same impersonation directly enables unauthorized use of authenticated state for merchant actions within the application, but no broader cross-authority compromise is evidenced); A:N (the evidence shows impersonation and unauthorized access, not direct service interruption).

Data flow

session["user_id"] -> session["restaurant_id"] -> session.get("user_id") -> db.get_user(user_id) -> current_user() is None

  • [ENTRY] session["user_id"] app/auth.py:22 login_user writes the authenticated user's id into Flask's cookie-backed session, creating the client-held authentication state later returned by the browser.
  • [FLOW] session["restaurant_id"] app/auth.py:23 login_user stores the tenant identifier in the same session object without additional binding beyond the session signature.
  • [FLOW] session.get("user_id") app/auth.py:32 current_user reads user_id from the returned session cookie on later requests, and this value is trusted if the session signature validates.
  • [FLOW] db.get_user(user_id) app/auth.py:33 The session-derived user_id selects the database record assigned to g.user, with no server-side session state checked here.
  • [SINK] current_user() is None app/auth.py:40 login_required allows access to protected views whenever the session-derived lookup yields a user object.
Prerequisites
  • MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET must be unset so the application uses the fallback secret identified in repository context.
  • The app must be using Flask's default signed cookie session behavior rather than a server-side session store.
  • The attacker is a remote web client crossing the boundary from unauthenticated HTTP traffic into authenticated merchant-session routes.
  • The forged cookie must contain values that satisfy downstream lookups, such as a valid user_id; restaurant_id also affects tenant context because it is stored in the same session.
  • This auth/session code is part of the normal application path, not an optional extension.

  • Of the provided related references, the generic CWE-798 hard-coded-key pattern is analogous; the listed CVE-2021-23336 concerns URL query parsing and is not the same pattern.
Description

Remove the known fallback session secret from configuration and require a deployment-provided high-entropy secret at startup. If this client-side session design is retained, keep only data in the cookie that the application is willing to trust under its signing model; alternatively, move authentication state to a server-side session store.

Suggested fix

MediumLikelyUse of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort in app/auth.py:_hash_passwordCWE-916auth.py
Description

app/auth.py derives a password verifier in _hash_password() by computing a single SHA-256 digest over salt + password at line 12, and verify_password() uses that value for comparison. The scanner flagged this as CWE-916 because SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash rather than a password-specific KDF. This becomes a security issue if stored password_hash and password_salt values are disclosed, allowing offline password guessing against the exported data.

Fileapp/auth.py
Line12
Impact (if exploitable)

If credential records are disclosed, an attacker can test password guesses at approximately the cost of one SHA-256 computation per candidate, using the stored per-user salt. This can increase the practicality of recovering weak or reused passwords from the exported hashes.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-916View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Model votes: 1 true positive, 0 false positive
  • Review limitation: The finding was reviewed by a single model (static-validator); there was no multi-model disagreement to compare.
  • Arguments supporting the finding:
    • _hash_password() at line 12 performs one hashlib.sha256(...) operation on the salted password.
    • Per-user salting prevents rainbow-table reuse, but does not add the computational cost associated with PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.
    • hmac.compare_digest() in verify_password() addresses timing behavior during comparison, not the cost of offline guessing after hash disclosure.
  • Arguments narrowing the scope:
    • Exploitation depends on prior disclosure of password_hash and password_salt values, such as through database, backup, or log exposure.
  • Unresolved disagreements: None were recorded.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 4.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:L (the evidenced harm is offline guessing against locally stored users-table password_hash/password_salt data; this item shows no network-reachable sink that by itself yields the cracking advantage); AC:L (given a disclosed row, the code uses one fast SHA-256 over salt+password, so candidate testing is straightforward and does not depend on races or unknown target state); PR:N (no pre-existing portal privileges are required to test guesses once the hash material is in hand); UI:N (no separate user must act for offline guessing to proceed); S:U (successful password recovery compromises credentials within the same application security authority); C:L (the direct evidenced impact is easier recovery of some users' passwords after hash disclosure, i.e. limited confidentiality loss); I:N (this helper does not directly modify application data or execute unauthorized actions); A:N (the evidence shows no direct effect on service availability).

Data flow

verify_password -> candidate -> hashlib.sha256

  • [ENTRY] verify_password app/auth.py:15 The login verification path receives a user-supplied password value for comparison against the stored credential.
  • [FLOW] candidate app/auth.py:17 verify_password forwards the supplied password together with user["password_salt"] into _hash_password without adding any work factor.
    • [FLAG] hashlib.sha256 app/auth.py:12 Inside _hash_password, the helper computes a single SHA-256 digest of salt plus password, which is the pattern the scanner identified.
Prerequisites
  • Deployment conditions: An attacker would need access to stored credential material, including both the password hash and the per-user salt.
  • Default vs optional code: This is application authentication code in app/auth.py, not an optional extension.
  • Trust boundary: The password input originates from the public login path (app/routes/auth_routes.py:16 per the trust-boundary context) and is compared against stored credential data. The main security boundary crossed for this finding is between externally supplied passwords and credential storage used later in offline attack scenarios.
  • Threat model/documentation context: The provided trust-boundary material identifies public login as an unauthenticated entry point. The supplied project context does not describe a password-hashing policy or indicate that fast hashing is intentional here.
  • Related CVE note: The listed CVE-2021-23336 concerns URL query parsing in urllib.parse and does not match the password-hashing pattern in this finding.
Callers
  • app/auth.py:verify_password
Description

In app/auth.py, update _hash_password at line 11 to derive password verifiers with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 and a substantial iteration count instead of a single SHA-256 over salt plus password.

Suggested fix
--- a/app/auth.py
+++ b/app/auth.py
@@ -8,8 +8,13 @@
8 from app import db
9
10
-def _hash_password(password, salt):
- return hashlib.sha256((salt + password).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
11+def _hash_password(password, salt):
12+ return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac(
13+ "sha256",
14+ password.encode("utf-8"),
15+ salt.encode("utf-8"),
16+ 600_000,
17+ ).hex()
18
19
20 def verify_password(user, password):
Rationale

PBKDF2 applies repeated keyed hashing to the password using the per-user salt, increasing the cost of each password guess so disclosed password hashes are materially harder to test offline than a single fast digest.

Verification

Before the change, hashing the same password and salt performs one SHA-256 and password candidates can be checked at near raw SHA-256 speed. After the change, the derived value should come from PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600000 iterations, verify_password should still return True for a record generated with the same KDF inputs, and any storage path that creates password_hash values should be updated to generate matching PBKDF2-based hashes.

search_menu_items builds a SQL SELECT statement by concatenating restaurant_id and the caller-supplied term into a LIKE clause, then executes the assembled string with db.execute(query) at app/db.py:99. Line30

Description

set_status() handles POST /orders/<int:order_id>/status, loads the current user from session-backed authentication at line 73, checks order["restaurant_id"] against user["restaurant_id"] at line 75, and then updates the order status at line 84. The scanner flagged this path because the tenant check relies on current_user(), and the finding context states Flask may fall back to a literal SECRET_KEY of "portal-dev-key". MediumLikelyCross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in app/routes/receipts.py:editorCWE-352receipts.py
Description

editor() handles GET and POST requests for /receipts and, on POST with action == "save", stores request.form["template"] for the current restaurant at app/routes/receipts.py:43. The finding was flagged because this state-changing branch shows no CSRF token validation, Origin/Referer check, or other request-origin verification in the provided code. This becomes a security issue if an attacker can cause a logged-in merchant’s browser to submit the POST with the merchant’s session cookie attached.

Fileapp/routes/receipts.py
Line43
Impact (if exploitable)

A cross-site request could overwrite the current restaurant’s stored receipt template without the merchant intentionally using the form. Because the template is later rendered by receipt flows in this file, the saved attacker-chosen content can affect subsequent receipt preview or printing behavior for that restaurant.

MediumLikelyUncaught Exception in app/services/pricing.py:normalize_priceCWE-248pricing.py
Description

normalize_price() parses user-supplied price strings into integer cents for menu item create/edit flows. The scanner flagged line 28 because Decimal(cleaned) accepts non-finite strings such as "NaN" and "Infinity", and the later comparison/quantize/int operations run outside the try/except that only handles parse failures. This becomes a security issue if an attacker can submit the price form field on the reachable create/edit routes; in the provided context, that boundary is an authenticated merchant session.

Fileapp/services/pricing.py
Line28
Impact (if exploitable)

If a caller submits a non-finite decimal string that survives parsing, create/edit processing can terminate with an uncaught server-side exception instead of returning a normalized price. In practice, that can cause the affected request to fail with a 500-style response and prevent the menu item update or creation from completing.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-248View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Review outcome in the provided transcript: 1 model classified the finding as a true positive, 0 as a false positive.
  • True-positive argument: Decimal(cleaned) accepts special non-finite values, so they bypass the except InvalidOperation block at lines 22-25; later operations on dollars are unguarded and can raise decimal exceptions.
  • Counterpoint raised in self-challenge: the current try/except might appear to cover malformed numeric input, and some later Decimal operations may not fail for every special value.
  • Remaining uncertainty noted in the transcript: the exact failing operation can vary by value and Decimal context (NaN vs Infinity), but the shared conclusion was that non-finite inputs can still reach an uncaught exception path.
  • Limitation: the debate evidence shown here is a single-model review transcript rather than a multi-model split discussion.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L, confidence: high) — AV:N (authenticated merchants reach the create/edit item handlers over HTTP and control the price field); AC:L (a non-finite price string like NaN or Infinity directly reaches normalize_price with no special environmental condition); PR:L (the affected create/edit routes are behind login_required); UI:N (the attacker submits the malformed form value themselves); S:U (the uncaught exception occurs inside the same Flask application authority); C:N (the evidence shows request failure, not data disclosure); I:N (the failing request prevents the save rather than directly modifying data); A:L (comparison, quantize, or int conversion on the non-finite Decimal can raise uncaught exceptions and make the create/edit request fail with a server error).

Data flow

create_item -> cleaned -> Decimal(cleaned) -> if dollars < 0 -> quantize

  • [ENTRY] create_item app/routes/menus.py:73 The authenticated menu creation route accepts the price form field from the request and passes it to the pricing helper.
    • [FLOW] cleaned app/services/pricing.py:19 The helper normalizes the raw user input into a string but does not reject non-finite decimal literals.
    • [FLOW] Decimal(cleaned) app/services/pricing.py:23 Parsing converts strings such as NaN or Infinity into Decimal objects instead of raising InvalidOperation.
    • [FLOW] if dollars < 0 app/services/pricing.py:26 The code continues with unguarded arithmetic and comparison on the parsed Decimal without checking that it is finite.
    • [FLAG] quantize app/services/pricing.py:28 The flagged line quantizes the derived cents value after the parse guard has already been left.

  • Reachable caller evidence was provided for app/routes/menus.py:73 create_item; the finding summary also lists edit_item as a caller.
  • Exploitation requires access to menu create/edit requests with control over the price form field.
  • Based on the trust-boundary data, this is an authenticated merchant input path, not a public unauthenticated route.
  • app/services/pricing.py is part of the application’s normal code path for price handling, not an optional extension.
  • The relevant trust boundary is low-trust form input crossing into server-side normalization logic.
  • The function’s docstring states that bad form values should return 0 so saves do not crash, but the implementation only catches InvalidOperation from Decimal(cleaned) and does not explicitly reject non-finite Decimal values afterward.
  • No related CVE references were provided in the finding context.
Callers
  • app/routes/menus.py:edit_item
  • app/routes/menus.py:create_item
Description

In app/services/pricing.py in normalize_price at line 23, reject non-finite Decimal values immediately after parsing by adding an is_finite() check before the comparison, quantize, and int conversion steps.

Suggested fix
--- a/app/services/pricing.py
+++ b/app/services/pricing.py
@@ -19,14 +19,16 @@
19 cleaned = str(raw).strip().lstrip("$").replace(",", "")
20 if not cleaned:
21 return 0
- try:
- dollars = Decimal(cleaned)
- except InvalidOperation:
- return 0
- if dollars < 0:
- dollars = Decimal(0)
- cents = (dollars * 100).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
- return int(cents)

23+ dollars = Decimal(cleaned)
24+ except InvalidOperation:

32
33

Rationale

Decimal() accepts special values such as NaN and Infinity as valid Decimals, so the existing InvalidOperation handler does not stop them. Returning early when dollars.is_finite() is false prevents those special values from reaching later arithmetic operations that can raise uncaught decimal exceptions.

Verification

Before the change, submit create/edit item requests with price values such as "Infinity" or "NaN" and observe that normalization can raise a server-side exception during processing. After the change, the same inputs should be handled by normalize_price returning 0 instead of raising, while ordinary finite prices such as "12.50" should still normalize to 1250.

MediumLikelyExecution with Unnecessary Privileges in Dockerfile:<global>CWE-250Dockerfile
Description

The Dockerfile builds the application image from python:3.11-slim and starts the app with CMD ["sh", "-c", "python migrations/init_db.py && python run.py"] at line 13. The scanner flagged that no USER instruction appears before CMD, so the container process inherits the base image default account, which is root for this image. This becomes a security issue if an attacker can already achieve code execution in the Flask process, because that code would then run as UID 0 inside the container rather than as a dedicated unprivileged user.

FileDockerfile
Line13
Impact (if exploitable)

If the prerequisites are met, code executing through the web process runs as root inside the container. That allows modification of application files under /app, the local SQLite database path referenced in the review context, and any writable mounted data. It also increases the consequences of any separate container escape or lateral-movement condition, though this finding alone does not imply host-level root access.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-250View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • True positive votes: 1 analyzer transcript, plus the validator score marked the finding as real (validator=100%, debate=100%, combined 100%)
  • False positive votes: 0
  • Arguments supporting the finding:
    • The Dockerfile contains no USER instruction before the final CMD, so runtime identity is inherited from python:3.11-slim.
    • The review notes a reachable in-repo server-side code-execution path through merchant-controlled Jinja template rendering in app/routes/receipts.py and app/routes/orders.py.
    • Running the web process as root increases what post-exploitation code can modify inside the container, including application files and local writable data.
  • Arguments raised against the finding:
    • Root inside a container is not the same as host root.
    • Operators can override the runtime user outside the image.
    • Exploitation depends on a separate application flaw, not the Dockerfile alone.
  • Unresolved points:
    • Whether deployment policy already enforces a non-root runtime user is not shown in the repository.
  • Review limitation:
    • The transcript shows a single analyzer with self-challenge rather than a visibly split multi-model debate.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:N (the item ties exploitation to authenticated merchant HTTP routes such as /receipts that accept attacker-controlled template text and render it server-side in the web process); AC:L (once that in-process execution path is reached, no extra race or external condition is needed because the Dockerfile never drops privileges before CMD); PR:L (the referenced receipt editor is available to any logged-in merchant session); UI:N (the attacker submits the template/render request directly); S:U (the resulting root-context execution affects the same containerized application authority rather than crossing into a separately secured authority); C:N (the demonstrated outcome is root-context write/control, not a shown disclosure to the attacker); I:H (with no USER instruction before CMD, successful in-process code execution runs as UID 0 and can fully modify application files and writable mounted data in the container); A:N (the evidence shows broad write capability but not a directly demonstrated service shutdown).

Data flow

FROM python:3.11-slim -> CMD

  • [FLOW] FROM python:3.11-slim Dockerfile:1 The build starts from a base image whose default runtime user is inherited unless a later USER instruction overrides it.
  • [FLAG] CMD Dockerfile:13 The flagged startup command appears before any user change, so the container will execute it under the inherited default account.
Prerequisites
  • Deployment conditions required:
    • The image must be run as built, without an external runtime override such as docker run --user, Kubernetes securityContext.runAsUser, or an equivalent entrypoint privilege drop.
    • An attacker must first obtain code execution inside the web process through another application issue.
  • Default vs optional code path:
    • This is the main Dockerfile for the application image, not an optional extension.
  • Trust boundary crossed:
    • The boundary is from a low-trust remote web user to code execution inside the containerized server process.
    • The supplied context identifies authenticated merchant routes as low trust and cites merchant-controlled receipt template rendering as one server-side execution path.
  • Threat model / documentation context:
    • The trust-boundary data describes authenticated merchant inputs as low trust.
    • No repository evidence was provided showing that running the container as root is an intentional requirement.
  • Related CVEs:
    • No related CVEs were listed in the provided finding context.
Description

In Dockerfile at the startup section around line 13, create a dedicated unprivileged account, change ownership of /app to that account, and add a USER instruction before CMD so the Flask process does not run as the image default user.

Suggested fix
--- a/Dockerfile
+++ b/Dockerfile
@@ -6,8 +6,12 @@
6 COPY merchant-portal/requirements.txt ./requirements.txt
7 RUN pip install --no-index --find-links=/app/wheelhouse --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
8
-COPY merchant-portal/ ./
-
-EXPOSE 5000
-
-CMD ["sh", "-c", "python migrations/init_db.py && python run.py"]
9+COPY merchant-portal/ ./
10+
11+RUN useradd --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin appuser \
12+ && chown -R appuser:appuser /app
13+USER appuser
14+
15+EXPOSE 5000
16+
17+CMD ["sh", "-c", "python migrations/init_db.py && python run.py"]
Rationale

Adding USER changes the runtime identity of the container process from the inherited root account to an unprivileged account. Chowning /app preserves the application's ability to initialize and write its local database while preventing server-side code execution in the web process from inheriting UID 0.

Verification

Build and start the image, then run id -u inside the running container or print os.getuid() from the Flask process. Before the change, the process reports 0 and an injected template payload executes as root. After the change, the process reports a non-zero UID, migrations still initialize the database under /app, and the same payload executes only with the unprivileged container account.

MediumLikelyUse of Hard-coded Credentials in migrations/init_db.py:seedCWE-798init_db.py

seed() initializes the SQLite database and inserts restaurant owner accounts into the users table. The scanner flagged line 74 because the seeded owner@noodlebot.io account is created from a literal password value, "noodle123", which is then hashed and stored for runtime authentication at line 80. This becomes a security issue if this bootstrap data is present in a deployed instance, the password is not rotated or invalidated, and the application's login route is reachable by unauthenticated users.

Filemigrations/init_db.py
Line74
Impact (if exploitable)

A remote user who knows the seeded email and password can authenticate as the restaurant owner account created by the migration. That would grant whatever application access is associated with that owner session, such as restaurant-specific menu, order, or receipt-management functionality.

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Models voting true positive: 1
  • Models voting false positive: 0
  • Review limitation: The provided debate transcript shows a single-model review rather than a multi-model disagreement set.

Technical points raised for the finding

  • The migration seeds a login-capable owner account with a fixed password.
  • The login flow is described as accepting email/password from unauthenticated users and authenticating against seeded records.
  • The debate transcript states the password is also documented in the repository README, which would further reduce secrecy if that documentation is present in deployed workflows.

Technical points raised against or narrowing the finding

  • The script may be intended for local or demo bootstrap only.

MediumLikelyUse of Hard-coded Credentials in app/routes/auth_routes.py:loginCWE-798auth_routes.py
Description

login() in app/routes/auth_routes.py verifies submitted credentials and, on success, calls auth.login_user(user) at line 22 to establish Flask session-backed identity. The finding is tied to configuration rather than the password check itself: if MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET is unset, Config.SECRET_KEY falls back to the predictable value portal-dev-key, so a forged Flask session cookie can be accepted as authentic. The scanner location was clamped to line 25, but the session-establishment call in the shown source is line 22.

Fileapp/routes/auth_routes.py
Line25
Impact (if exploitable)

A remote client that knows the fallback secret can create a signed session cookie containing a chosen user identifier and have the application treat that session as authenticated. Resulting access would depend on the privileges of the forged user_id, and could expose or modify merchant-scoped functionality that relies on session identity.

Security impact
SeverityMedium

Exploitation is plausible but constrained by environmental or contextual factors.

Weakness IDCWE-798View details >
Debate summaryTrue positive
  • Available review result: 1 model argued true positive, 0 argued false positive; the provided transcript is single-sided rather than a multi-model disagreement.
  • Main technical argument: Flask signed-cookie session integrity depends on SECRET_KEY, authenticated routes trust session state such as the stored user identity, and the shipped fallback portal-dev-key is predictable if deployment leaves MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET unset.
  • Qualifier raised in the self-challenge: this depends on deployment configuration. If operators set a unique secret, forged cookies signed with the fallback value would not validate.
  • No opposing code-level argument was provided in the transcript.
  • The related-reference section lists a CWE-798 hard-coded-credentials KB pattern; no specific CVE was provided.
Severity rationale

CVSS v3.1 base score 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:N (public HTTP routes are reachable remotely and Flask accepts the attacker-supplied session cookie over that network path); AC:L (if the fallback SECRET_KEY is active, forging a valid signed session with a chosen user_id requires no race or special target state); PR:N (the attacker needs no prior account because current_user() and login_required trust session['user_id'] from the cookie); UI:N (the attacker sends their own forged cookie and requests authenticated routes directly); S:U (the forged session is trusted within the same Flask app and SQLite-backed authority); C:L (the forged authenticated session grants unauthorized access to merchant dashboard/menu/order/receipt data for the impersonated user); I:L (the same impersonation lets the attacker invoke authenticated create/edit/status actions as that user); A:N (the evidence shows authentication bypass via session forgery, not direct service disruption).

login -> auth.verify_password -> auth.login_user

  • [ENTRY] login app/routes/auth_routes.py:16 An unauthenticated client reaches the login handler, which is one place where the application establishes authenticated session state.
  • [FLOW] auth.verify_password app/routes/auth_routes.py:21 The submitted credentials are validated here, but no check on SECRET_KEY strength or uniqueness occurs in this path.
  • [FLAG] auth.login_user app/routes/auth_routes.py:22 The handler writes user identity into Flask session state that will later be accepted if signed with the configured secret key.
Prerequisites

    • MERCHANT_PORTAL_SECRET is unset.
    • The app uses Flask’s signed-cookie session mechanism with that fallback secret.
    • An attacker can send HTTP requests with a crafted session cookie.
  • Default vs optional:
    • The finding summary states app/__init__.py loads Config unconditionally.
    • The unsafe secret is described as the default when the operator does nothing, not as an optional extension.
  • Trust boundary:
    • Public HTTP clients are unauthenticated at entry.
    • Merchant routes later trust session-backed identity.
    • The boundary crossed is between attacker-controlled cookie data and server-trusted authenticated session state when the signing key is predictable.
  • Project context:
    • The trust-boundary notes describe public HTTP routes and authenticated merchant routes that rely on session state from app/auth.py.
    • The security-context notes say the bootstrap appears aimed at local/demo setup, so exposure depends on deployment hygiene.
Description

Remove the predictable fallback for SECRET_KEY and require a deployment-specific unpredictable secret at startup, or gate any development-only default so it cannot be used outside a development environment. The login() session write is by design; the issue described here is the surrounding configuration that determines whether those session cookies can be forged.

Description

seed() provisions initial users records during database initialization and includes literal owner passwords in the shipped account list at lines 73-74. The flagged behavior is that these values are hashed and stored as active login verifiers at line 80, so a fresh deployment created from this script will accept known default credentials until they are changed. Line73

An actor who knows the shipped passwords could authenticate as the seeded restaurant owner accounts on a freshly initialized instance. That would grant whatever access those owner accounts have to merchant session routes and associated restaurant data/functions until the credentials are rotated or the accounts are removed.

LowLikelyGeneration of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers in hash1lib.py:hash1lib.build_customer_survey_urlCWE-340hash1lib.py

hash1lib.build_customer_survey_url() builds a survey URL and derives its sig parameter as sha256("caldova:{order_id}") at hash1lib.py:13. The scanner flagged this because the digest is computed only from a predictable order_id and constant text, without a server-held secret. This becomes a security issue if downstream code or the external survey service treats sig as proof that the URL was minted by the application; the provided context does not include that downstream verification logic.

Filehash1lib.py
Line13
Impact (if exploitable)

If sig is accepted downstream as evidence that the URL is legitimate, a party that knows or can guess an order_id could generate matching survey links, replay previously valid-looking links, or substitute order identifiers while keeping a recomputed sig. The helper also exposes the raw order_id and derived sig to a third-party HTTP endpoint.

Security impact
SeverityLow

Lower exploitability or impact, but still worth remediating for defense-in-depth.

Weakness IDCWE-340View details >

  • True positive votes: 1
  • False positive votes: 0
  • Review limitation: The debate transcript shows a single-model review rather than a multi-model disagreement.

Arguments noted in the review:

  • The flagged line computes signature from public, guessable input only.
  • Anyone who knows or guesses an order_id can reproduce the same digest offline.
  • The helper labels and uses the value as a signature-like authenticity token in the returned URL.

Open point raised in the review:

  • The repository does not include the external survey service, so the evidence does not show whether that service actually enforces sig as an authorization or integrity check.

build_customer_survey_url -> signature -> build_customer_survey_url return

LowLikelyUse of a One-Way Hash with a Predictable Salt in migrations/init_db.py:seedCWE-760init_db.py
Description

migrations/init_db.py is a bootstrap script that recreates the SQLite database and seeds initial restaurant and user records. In seed(), the scanner flagged line 80 because the stored password hashes are derived from fixed 4-character salt literals defined in source ("b021" and "ndle"), so the same seeded accounts receive the same salts each time the script is run. This becomes security-relevant if the seeded accounts remain in use and an attacker can obtain the password database or otherwise perform offline analysis of the stored verifiers.

Filemigrations/init_db.py
Line80
Impact (if exploitable)

If the prerequisites are met, the seeded password records are easier to analyze offline than records salted with unique high-entropy values. The same seeded salts can be reused across deployments initialized by this script, which allows precomputation or targeted cracking work to carry over between installations that keep these default accounts.

  • Arguments raised against it: salts do not need to be secret, the two seeded accounts do use different salts, and the seeded passwords are already hardcoded, which limits the additional risk introduced by salt predictability alone.
  • Unresolved points: the debate did not dispute the code pattern, but the practical impact depends on whether these demo/bootstrap accounts survive into an attacker-reachable deployment.

LowLikelyUse of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort in migrations/init_db.py:seedCWE-916init_db.py
Description

seed() inserts bootstrap user records into the users table, and line 80 stores hash_password(password, salt) for each seeded account. The flagged behavior is that hash_password() at line 58 uses a single SHA-256(salt + password) digest rather than a password KDF with a tunable cost. This becomes security-relevant if the seeded database is used for live authentication and an attacker can obtain the stored verifiers for offline guessing; the code path itself is local bootstrap code, not a public request handler.

Filemigrations/init_db.py
Line80
Impact (if exploitable)

If the stored users.password_hash values are disclosed, password guesses against these seeded accounts can be tested at the cost of a single SHA-256 computation per guess rather than a slower password KDF. If plaintext passwords are recovered and the accounts remain active, those credentials could then be used to authenticate as the seeded restaurant users.

  • Arguments noted against broader impact:

Rationale

PBKDF2 applies the password hash many times with a defined work factor, so each offline password guess is materially more expensive than a single fast SHA-256 evaluation. This changes the stored verifier from a general-purpose digest to a password-derived key intended for authentication storage.

Verification

Before the change, initialize the database and observe that a seeded row's password_hash equals hashlib.sha256((salt + password).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest() for the known seeded credentials. After the change, reinitialize the database and verify that the same comparison no longer matches, while logging in with the seeded email/password still succeeds because both seeding and verification use the updated hash_password() implementation.

LowLikelyActive Debug Code in run.py:<top-level>CWE-489run.py
Description

run.py reads startup settings from environment variables and passes them to Flask.app.run(). The scanner flagged line 10 because DEBUG defaults to "true" when unset, so the application starts with debug=True unless the operator overrides it. This becomes a security issue if this startup path is used outside development and the resulting server is exposed beyond the default loopback bind.

Filerun.py
Line10
Impact (if exploitable)

If this code path is used in an exposed deployment with DEBUG unset, the application runs with Flask debug behavior rather than a hardened production baseline. Depending on the runtime and exposure, that can include detailed error output and debugger-related functionality that is intended for development use.

Security impact
SeverityLow

Lower exploitability or impact, but still worth remediating for defense-in-depth.

  • The counterpoint raised within the same review was contextual: HOST defaults to 127.0.0.1, and DEBUG is operator-controlled configuration rather than remote request input.
  • The finding was effectively unchallenged in the provided debate material; the transcript contains a single model review, so there was no multi-model disagreement to compare.

CVSS v3.1 base score 0.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:N, confidence: medium) — AV:L (the demonstrated trigger is local startup of run.py with environment-derived settings, specifically DEBUG unset so it defaults true); AC:L (the code deterministically enables debug mode from the default value with no external condition); PR:L (the actor must control the local startup environment or invocation of the process); UI:N (no separate victim action is needed to enable the mode); S:U (the same Flask application is started in debug mode under the same security authority); C:N (the evidence here shows only debug-mode enablement, not a specific direct disclosure to an attacker); I:N (no demonstrated unauthorized modification or code execution is provided in this item); A:N (no direct availability impact is shown).

os.environ.get("DEBUG", "true") -> app.run

  • [SINK] app.run run.py:11 The computed boolean is supplied to Flask's runtime startup call, enabling debug mode when the default path is used.
Prerequisites
  • The application must be started through run.py or equivalent code path that executes this block.

Description

In run.py at line 10 in the top-level startup block, change the DEBUG environment fallback from "true" to "false" so Flask debug mode is disabled unless it is explicitly enabled.

Suggested fix
--- a/run.py
+++ b/run.py
@@ -7,5 +7,5 @@
7 if __name__ == "__main__":
8 host = os.environ.get("HOST", "127.0.0.1")
9 port = int(os.environ.get("PORT", "5000"))
- debug = os.environ.get("DEBUG", "true").lower() in {"1", "true", "yes", "on"}
10+ debug = os.environ.get("DEBUG", "false").lower() in {"1", "true", "yes", "on"}
11 app.run(host=host, port=port, debug=debug)
Rationale

Using a safe default changes the startup baseline so an unset DEBUG variable no longer turns on Flask's debugger and other development behavior; the application only enters debug mode when an operator opts in through configuration.

Verification

Start the application with DEBUG unset. Before the change, the computed debug value is True and Flask starts in debug mode. After the change, the computed debug value is False when DEBUG is unset, while setting DEBUG=true still enables debug mode explicitly.
